text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Understanding Menopause Understand menopause, common symptoms, when to seek medical advice and how a GP can help you review treatment and long-term health. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Menopause is a normal life stage, but the transition can affect people very differently. Symptoms may begin during perimenopause and can include hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, mood changes, vaginal or urinary symptoms and changes in periods. Why This Topic Matters Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a menstrual period, provided there is no other explanation. The transition can affect sleep, temperature regulation, sexual wellbeing and longer-term bone health; experiences vary widely. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, mood changes and interrupted sleep are common reasons for discussion. Unexplained bleeding after menopause needs assessment rather than attribution to hormonal change. Symptoms interfere with sleep, work or relationships. You develop bleeding after 12 months without a period. You want to weigh hormone therapy and non-hormonal options against personal risks. Menopause is more than the final menstrual period Menopause is reached after 12 months without a menstrual period when there is no other explanation. The years leading up to it are called perimenopause, when periods and symptoms can become less predictable. A useful consultation looks at symptoms, age, menstrual history, contraception needs, personal and family history, cardiovascular and bone health, medicines and what matters most to you. Treatment is individual and may include lifestyle measures, non-hormonal options or menopause hormone therapy when appropriate. Keep a record of symptoms and menstrual changes if helpful Discuss abnormal or unexpected bleeding rather than assuming it is menopause Ask about contraception until menopause is confirmed Review bone, heart and preventive health as part of midlife care When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book medical advice if symptoms are affecting sleep, mood, work, relationships or quality of life. Any vaginal bleeding after menopause should be medically assessed. Severe or rapidly worsening symptoms also deserve prompt review. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess symptoms, consider other possible causes, discuss treatment choices and contraindications, review preventive health, and refer to a gynaecologist or other clinician when specialist input is appropriate. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between perimenopause and menopause? Perimenopause is the transition leading up to menopause. Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a period when there is no other cause. Do I always need a blood test to diagnose menopause? Not always. In many people the diagnosis is based on age, symptoms and menstrual history. Testing may be useful in particular circumstances. Can a GP discuss menopause hormone therapy? Yes. A GP can discuss potential benefits, risks and alternatives and determine whether further assessment or specialist input is needed. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health When Should I Have A Cervical Screening Test? Understand current Australian cervical screening intervals, self-collection options and when symptoms need assessment rather than routine screening. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Australia’s National Cervical Screening Program uses HPV testing to reduce the risk of cervical cancer. For most eligible women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 74, routine screening is recommended every five years, but individual circumstances can change what is appropriate. Why This Topic Matters Cervical screening looks for HPV associated with cervical cancer, rather than waiting for symptoms. Under the National Cervical Screening Program, most eligible people with a cervix aged 25–74 are invited every five years; individual follow-up can differ after an abnormal result. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Routine screening is intended for people without symptoms. Bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, bleeding after menopause or unusual persistent discharge warrants assessment even if your screening is up to date. You are due for routine screening or unsure when your last test was. You would like to discuss self-collection and clinician collection. You have symptoms that need diagnostic assessment, not just routine screening. Routine screening and symptom assessment are not the same thing The Cervical Screening Test checks for human papillomavirus (HPV), which can cause cervical cell changes. Eligible participants can discuss clinician-collected and self-collected sampling options with their healthcare provider. Routine screening is designed for people without symptoms. Symptoms such as unusual vaginal bleeding, bleeding after sex, persistent unusual discharge or pelvic symptoms should be discussed with a clinician even if your next routine screening test is not due. Most eligible participants are invited from age 25 to 74 Routine interval is generally five years when previous results and circumstances allow Self-collection is an option for eligible participants under the national program Previous abnormal results, immune conditions or other clinical factors can change follow-up When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP if you are unsure when you are due, have received an abnormal result, have symptoms such as unusual bleeding or discharge, or need help choosing a collection option. Significant bleeding, severe pain or rapidly worsening symptoms may need urgent assessment. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can confirm your screening history, explain current eligibility, arrange or perform screening, discuss self-collection, interpret results and coordinate follow-up or specialist referral if needed. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Is the Cervical Screening Test the same as the old Pap smear? The current program primarily tests for HPV rather than looking first for abnormal cells, although people still commonly use the term Pap smear. Can I collect my own sample? Eligible participants can choose self-collection under the National Cervical Screening Program. Your healthcare provider can explain whether it is suitable for you. Should I wait for my screening date if I have symptoms? No. Symptoms need clinical assessment and should not be delayed until the next routine screening test. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Women's Health Checks At Different Stages Of Life A stage-by-stage guide to preventive women’s healthcare, including screening, reproductive health, vaccination and midlife health discussions. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction There is no single ‘women’s health check’ that is right for everyone. Preventive care changes with age, symptoms, reproductive plans, family history, previous results and health risks. Why This Topic Matters Preventive priorities change with age, pregnancy plans, medications, medical history and personal circumstances. A useful review addresses individual risk rather than giving every patient the same package of tests. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Discussions may involve menstrual health, contraception, pregnancy planning, cervical screening, cardiovascular risk, menopause symptoms or bone health. Family history can change screening and referral decisions. You are planning pregnancy or considering contraception. You have new menstrual, breast or menopause symptoms. Your family history or screening status has changed. Preventive care changes as your priorities change In younger adulthood, consultations may focus on contraception, sexual health, vaccination, mental health and cervical screening when eligible. Pregnancy planning can add folate, medicines review, vaccination and chronic condition optimisation. Midlife care may include menopause symptoms, cardiovascular risk, bone health and screening. Later-life care can increasingly focus on mobility, medicines, chronic conditions, falls risk, vaccination and maintaining independence. Cervical screening according to the national program Breast awareness and age-appropriate breast screening discussions Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment Vaccination and sexual health when relevant Pregnancy planning, menopause or healthy ageing according to life stage When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP appointment if you are unsure which preventive checks apply to you, have new symptoms, have a strong family history or are entering a new life stage such as pregnancy planning or menopause. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review your individual risk profile and screening history, identify what is due, avoid unnecessary testing, discuss prevention and coordinate referrals to screening programs or specialists where appropriate. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need an annual full blood test? Not necessarily. Tests should be based on symptoms, age, risk factors and clinical need rather than a fixed yearly panel for everyone. Are screening programs the same for every person? No. National programs provide age and risk guidance, but previous results, symptoms and individual history may alter recommendations. Can preventive care be discussed during a routine GP visit? Yes. Depending on time and complexity, your GP can review prevention during a routine visit or recommend a dedicated longer appointment. title: Perimenopause Guide
description: Learn what perimenopause is, common symptoms, when to see a GP and how treatment and contraception can be discussed.

Perimenopause can affect periods, sleep, mood and wellbeing

text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Understanding Perimenopause Learn what perimenopause is, common symptoms, when to see a GP and how treatment and contraception can be discussed. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Perimenopause is the transition before menopause. Hormone levels can fluctuate, periods may change and symptoms can come and go for several years. Because the pattern varies widely, care should be guided by the individual rather than a fixed list of symptoms. Why This Topic Matters Perimenopause is the time of hormonal change leading up to menopause. Cycle changes may begin years before the final period, and pregnancy remains possible while ovulation continues. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Periods may become irregular, heavier or lighter; hot flushes, headaches, sleep disruption and mood changes may occur. Very heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods or bleeding after sex should be assessed independently of age. Bleeding becomes heavy, prolonged or unpredictable. Symptoms affect wellbeing or you are uncertain about contraception. You are younger than expected for menopause or have new symptoms needing assessment. Perimenopause can affect periods, sleep, mood and wellbeing Common experiences include changes in menstrual timing or flow, hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, vaginal dryness, mood changes, anxiety, reduced concentration and joint or muscle symptoms. Pregnancy is still possible during perimenopause. Contraception, pregnancy intentions and treatment choices should therefore be considered together. Symptoms under age 45, very heavy bleeding or unusual bleeding patterns may need additional assessment. Track period changes and symptoms if this helps identify a pattern Do not assume every symptom is hormonal Discuss contraception while pregnancy remains possible Raise heavy, prolonged or otherwise unusual bleeding with a clinician When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP if symptoms are difficult to manage, affect daily life, begin unusually early, or if bleeding is heavy, prolonged, occurs after sex or is otherwise concerning. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess whether symptoms fit perimenopause, consider alternative explanations, discuss contraception and treatment options, and review longer-term bone, heart and preventive health. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Can perimenopause start while I still have regular periods? Symptoms can begin before periods stop completely, although menstrual changes are common as the transition progresses. Can I still become pregnant during perimenopause? Yes. Pregnancy remains possible until menopause is confirmed, so discuss contraception if you do not want to become pregnant. Are hormone blood tests always needed? No. Assessment is often based on age, symptoms and menstrual history. Testing is more useful in selected circumstances. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Preventive Women's Healthcare Understand how preventive women’s healthcare brings together screening, vaccination, cardiovascular health, reproductive care and mental wellbeing. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Preventive women’s healthcare is not a single appointment or test. It is an ongoing process of matching screening, vaccination and risk reduction to your age, history, symptoms and life stage. Why This Topic Matters Prevention includes screening when eligible, vaccination, addressing lifestyle risks and acting on symptoms. Tests without a clear indication may cause unnecessary worry or follow-up, so decisions should be individualised. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Relevant situations include overdue cervical screening, questions about breast screening, changes in blood pressure, diabetes risks and vaccination planning. A new symptom requires its own assessment; screening is not a substitute. You are unsure which screening invitations apply to your age. You have strong family history of cancer, heart disease or diabetes. You are entering a new life stage and want to review health priorities. Prevention works best when care is connected A GP can help bring together cervical screening, breast health, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, vaccination, sexual and reproductive health, mental wellbeing, pregnancy planning, menopause and healthy ageing. The aim is not to perform every possible test. It is to identify what is recommended, what is clinically useful now and what can safely wait, while keeping future follow-up visible. Keep screening and vaccination history up to date Review medicines before pregnancy or when health circumstances change Discuss family history that may alter screening decisions Use routine visits to revisit prevention over time When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a preventive health discussion if you are unsure what is due, have missed screening, have a significant family history or are preparing for pregnancy, menopause or another life transition. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can personalise prevention, check national screening recommendations, assess risk factors, discuss lifestyle and reproductive health, and arrange tests or referrals that are clinically indicated. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions What should a preventive health appointment include? It depends on your age and individual risks. It may include screening history, blood pressure, vaccination, lifestyle, reproductive health and other targeted checks. Is more testing always better? No. Preventive care aims for appropriate evidence-based screening and risk assessment, not indiscriminate testing. Can family history change what I need? Yes. Some family histories can change the timing or type of screening, so tell your GP about important conditions in close relatives. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Men's Health Health Checks Every Man Should Consider A practical guide to men’s preventive health checks, risk assessment and why screening should be tailored to age and personal history. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction There is no universal checklist of tests that every man needs every year. Good preventive care is based on age, symptoms, family history, lifestyle, previous results and existing medical conditions. Why This Topic Matters A preventive consultation can address cardiovascular risk, smoking, alcohol use, weight, activity, vaccinations and age-appropriate screening. The goal is to choose checks based on medical history rather than order every possible blood test. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Consider a review if you have raised blood pressure, family history of early heart disease, changes in urination, persistent fatigue or concerns about sexual wellbeing. Some important risks, such as high blood pressure, cause no symptoms. You have not reviewed blood pressure or cardiovascular risk recently. You have new urinary symptoms or a concerning family history. You want a practical plan for screening, vaccinations or lifestyle changes. Start with risk, not a generic test panel A preventive health review may include blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, diabetes risk, vaccination, bowel screening, skin health, mental wellbeing, smoking and alcohol use, weight and physical activity. Prostate discussions may be relevant depending on age, symptoms, family history and preferences. The value of regular GP care is that these areas can be reviewed together. Tests can then be ordered for a clear reason rather than simply repeated by habit. Know your blood pressure and cardiovascular risk Participate in recommended national screening programs Discuss family history of prostate, bowel, heart and other disease Keep vaccinations up to date Raise mental health, sleep, sexual health or urinary symptoms early When Should I Seek Medical Advice? PSA testing is a preference-sensitive decision involving discussion of potential benefits, false alarms and overdiagnosis. Blood in urine, fever with urinary problems or inability to pass urine requires prompt or urgent evaluation. Urination changes are persistent or worsening. You have a family history of prostate cancer and want tailored risk advice. You want to discuss whether PSA testing is suitable for you. Prostate assessment depends on symptoms, age and individual risk Symptoms such as a weak urine stream, difficulty starting, frequent urination, urgency or getting up often at night can occur with prostate enlargement and other urinary conditions. A GP may ask about the pattern, medicines, infections and other health factors. PSA blood testing can be useful in selected people, but it is not a simple yes-or-no cancer test. Before testing, it is useful to discuss what an elevated result can mean, possible follow-up and your personal risk factors, including family history. What does a high PSA mean? PSA can be raised for several reasons. An elevated result usually requires interpretation and sometimes repeat testing or specialist assessment rather than proving cancer by itself. Looking at overall risk is more useful than focusing on one number in isolation. Why This Topic Matters Cardiovascular risk depends on more than cholesterol alone. Blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, kidney health, age and family history can all affect an individual prevention plan. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Heart disease may not cause warning symptoms until an event occurs. Chest pressure, sweating, shortness of breath, fainting or pain spreading to the arm or jaw can signal an emergency and need immediate help. You smoke, have high blood pressure or diabetes, or have a strong family history. You would like a formal cardiovascular risk assessment. Chest pain or symptoms of a heart attack require 000, not routine booking. Cardiovascular risk can often be identified before symptoms appear A GP can review blood pressure, smoking status, family history, diabetes risk, relevant blood tests and other factors to estimate cardiovascular risk and discuss prevention. Lifestyle changes and medicines may be recommended depending on the result. Symptoms such as chest pressure, severe shortness of breath, collapse or sudden neurological symptoms are not routine preventive issues and need urgent emergency assessment. Understand fever in children, warning signs that need urgent assessment and when a GP review may be appropriate. Fever is common with infections, but the temperature number is only part of the assessment. A child’s age, breathing, alertness, hydration and other symptoms are also important. Why This Topic Matters Fever is a sign that the body is responding to illness, not a diagnosis. A child’s age, breathing, hydration, alertness and overall appearance are often more informative than the temperature alone. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Warning signs include breathing difficulty, marked drowsiness, dehydration, a non-blanching rash or a seizure. Any baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment. A baby younger than three months has a fever of 38°C or more. Your child is unusually sleepy, struggles to breathe or cannot keep fluids down. If very unwell or unresponsive, call 000. Look at the child, not only the thermometer Children with fever may be tired, irritable, shivery or less interested in food and drink. Most fevers are caused by infections, but some children need urgent assessment because of their age or accompanying symptoms. Babies under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher need prompt medical assessment. In any age group, difficulty breathing, unusual drowsiness, a first seizure, blue or very pale colour, a concerning rash or signs of severe dehydration require urgent attention. Measure temperature with an appropriate thermometer Encourage fluids and watch urine output Pay attention to breathing, alertness and behaviour Do not rely on whether fever medicine lowers the temperature to decide how serious the illness is When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 or seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, unresponsiveness, blue colour, a first seizure or another life-threatening concern. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess the child’s history, hydration, breathing and other symptoms, examine for a likely source of infection and decide whether tests, treatment or hospital assessment are needed. No. Severity depends on the child’s age, symptoms and overall condition as well as temperature. When is fever an emergency? Emergency assessment is needed for signs such as severe breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, blue colour, a first seizure or other serious deterioration. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Children's Health Common Childhood Illnesses An overview of common childhood illnesses, what parents can monitor at home and warning signs that need medical assessment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Coughs, colds, gastroenteritis, sore throats, ear symptoms, rashes and fevers are common in childhood. Many illnesses improve with supportive care, but children can change quickly and the same symptom can have different causes. Why This Topic Matters Children often experience coughs, colds, gastroenteritis and ear infections, especially when starting childcare or school. Many are viral, so antibiotics are not routinely helpful. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Watch for poor fluid intake, reduced wet nappies, high work of breathing, persistent pain or a child who seems much less responsive than usual. The pattern of illness and age guide the urgency of assessment. Your child is worsening instead of gradually recovering. There is breathing difficulty, dehydration or persistent severe pain. Symptoms recur frequently or you are unsure whether school or childcare attendance is safe. The child’s overall condition helps guide urgency When a child is unwell, monitor breathing, alertness, fluid intake, urine output, temperature and whether symptoms are improving or worsening. Younger infants and children with significant medical conditions may need assessment earlier. Antibiotics are not useful for most viral illnesses. A clinical assessment can help identify when bacterial infection, dehydration, asthma, pneumonia, ear infection or another condition should be considered. Offer fluids regularly Watch for breathing difficulty or dehydration Note the duration and pattern of symptoms Avoid giving medicines that are not age-appropriate or have not been recommended When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP when symptoms are persistent, worsening or concerning, especially with poor drinking, reduced urine, breathing changes, severe pain or unusual rash. Call 000 for severe breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, blue colour or another life-threatening emergency. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can examine the child, identify likely causes, advise on supportive care, prescribe treatment when clinically indicated and explain what warning signs should trigger further review. Families from Woolloongabba, Dutton Park, Stones Corner and surrounding areas can use general practice as a familiar first point of care for many childhood health concerns. Frequently Asked Questions Do children with colds need antibiotics? Usually not. Colds are commonly viral, and antibiotics do not treat viruses. How can I tell if my child is dehydrated? Reduced drinking, fewer wet nappies or less urine, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness and lack of tears can be warning signs. Should a rash always be seen by a doctor? Many rashes are mild, but a new rash with fever, significant illness, breathing difficulty or rapid progression deserves prompt assessment. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Children's Health Children's Preventive Healthcare Understand preventive healthcare for children, including vaccination, growth, development, family risk and healthy routines. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Preventive healthcare for children supports healthy growth and development while keeping vaccinations and age-appropriate checks visible. It works best when preventive needs are reviewed alongside ordinary illness visits rather than only when something is wrong. Why This Topic Matters Preventive child health combines immunisation, developmental surveillance, oral health, nutrition, sleep and safe physical activity. Concerns can arise even when a child is otherwise well. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Consider a review for missed vaccinations, uncertainty about development, growth changes, hearing or vision concerns, and difficulties with school participation or sleep. You have concerns about speech, learning, growth or behaviour. Your child is due for immunisations or has missed routine care. Family or teachers have noticed a sustained change in functioning. Prevention follows development over time Depending on age and circumstances, preventive care may include vaccination, growth and development, nutrition, sleep, dental health, vision or hearing concerns, physical activity, school health, mental wellbeing and family history. There is no need to perform every test on every child. A GP can identify concerns from history, examination and developmental context and arrange targeted assessment when needed. Keep immunisation records current Raise concerns about development, hearing, vision or learning early Discuss nutrition, sleep and activity as part of health Update the GP about important family history When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a review if you have concerns about growth, development, behaviour, school functioning, nutrition, sleep, vaccination or recurrent illness. Sudden severe illness still requires urgent assessment rather than a preventive visit. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can track health over time, review vaccination and development, assess concerns, support healthy routines and coordinate paediatric, allied health or other referrals when appropriate. Families from Woolloongabba, Dutton Park, Stones Corner and surrounding areas can use general practice as a familiar first point of care for many childhood health concerns. Frequently Asked Questions Does every child need routine blood tests? No. Blood tests are generally based on symptoms, risk factors or a specific clinical question. Can a GP discuss developmental concerns? Yes. A GP can assess the concern and arrange further developmental or paediatric review when needed. Is vaccination part of preventive care? Yes. Keeping vaccinations current is an important part of childhood preventive healthcare. Trusted Australian information For further general information, these national health resources may be useful. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Children's Health Managing Winter Respiratory Illness Understand common winter coughs, colds and flu, when home care may help and which symptoms require GP or urgent review. Introduction Winter can bring more respiratory illness as people spend time indoors. Viruses such as influenza, RSV and other cold viruses may cause cough, sore throat, fever and fatigue. Most mild viral illnesses improve with time and supportive care, but some patients need closer monitoring. Why This Topic Matters Young babies, older adults, pregnant people and those with certain medical conditions can be at higher risk of complications. Antibiotics do not treat uncomplicated viral infections; assessment helps distinguish expected recovery from pneumonia, dehydration or another problem. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: Cough, congestion, sore throat, body aches or a fever affecting usual activity. Worsening breathlessness, chest discomfort, reduced drinking or signs of dehydration. Symptoms that improve then worsen again, or fever that persists unexpectedly. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP review for persistent fever, worsening cough or additional risk factors, and ask whether testing or antiviral medicines may be relevant. Seek urgent help for marked breathing difficulty, blue lips, confusion, severe dehydration or a seriously unwell baby; call 000 for life-threatening signs. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess breathing and hydration, examine you when needed, and guide treatment or testing. They can advise about staying home while contagious, symptom relief, vaccination and when to return for review. Children and older adults may need different thresholds for reassessment. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Will antibiotics help my winter cough? Most winter respiratory infections are viral, so antibiotics do not help unless a bacterial infection is suspected or confirmed. Should I attend in person with respiratory symptoms? Contact the clinic first if you have infectious symptoms so the team can advise on safe attendance and appointment options. Can influenza vaccination still help during winter? Yes. It may still be worthwhile during the season depending on individual recommendations and vaccine availability. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Breast Health: Changes, Screening & When To See A GP Learn which breast changes need assessment, how BreastScreen Australia works and why symptoms need diagnostic review. Introduction Breast health involves understanding what is normal for your body, noticing changes and using screening appropriately. A new breast symptom should be assessed even if a recent screening mammogram was normal; screening and investigating symptoms serve different purposes. Why This Topic Matters BreastScreen Australia invites eligible women aged 50–74 for a free mammogram every two years. Women aged 40–49 and 75 or older may also access free screening, but are generally not routinely invited. Family history and symptoms may change the recommended pathway. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A new lump or thickened area in a breast or armpit. Nipple discharge, especially if bloody, or a newly inverted nipple. Persistent skin dimpling, redness, swelling or a change in breast shape. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Arrange a GP appointment promptly for a new lump, persistent breast change or unexplained nipple discharge. Do not wait for the next routine BreastScreen invitation. Sudden severe infection symptoms or rapidly worsening illness may require urgent care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can take a history, examine the area, review family risk and arrange appropriate imaging or referral when indicated. Your clinician can also explain routine screening eligibility. Screening mammograms are not a substitute for diagnostic investigation of a new symptom. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need to wait until age 50 for a breast screen? Women aged 40–49 may access free BreastScreen mammography, but screening decisions should take individual risks into account. I had a normal mammogram. Should I ignore a new lump? No. A new lump or change requires assessment even after normal screening. Are all breast lumps cancer? No. Many are benign, but examination and, where needed, imaging are important to identify the cause. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Healthy Ageing Healthy Ageing: Prevention, Falls, Vaccination & Reviews Practical healthy-ageing advice about fall prevention, vaccination, medicines and GP health reviews for older adults. Introduction Healthy ageing is about staying as well and independent as possible, not simply treating diseases after they appear. Changes in strength, balance, hearing, memory or medicines can affect everyday activities, so preventive reviews should consider the whole person. Why This Topic Matters Falls can lead to injuries and loss of confidence, while complex medicine regimens can increase side effects. Vaccinations and age-appropriate screening can reduce specific risks. Plans work best when they reflect the person's own priorities, living circumstances and support network. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A recent fall, near-fall, dizziness or new hesitation about walking outdoors. Unexpected weight loss, reduced strength, memory concerns or difficulty managing medicines. Uncertainty about influenza, shingles, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccinations. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP review after a fall, when daily function is changing, or when a medicine causes dizziness or confusion. Sudden weakness on one side, facial droop, new speech difficulty or acute confusion may indicate an emergency: call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess fall risks, blood pressure, vision and medicine effects, discuss exercise and bone health, and consider physiotherapy or other support. They may recommend a relevant health assessment, personalised vaccination review or tests based on medical history. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Are falls just part of getting older? No. Falls have many potential contributors, and identifying modifiable risks can make a difference. Should older people have a medicine review? A review is especially useful after falls, side effects, hospital discharge or multiple prescription changes. Is every vaccine funded for all older adults? No. Recommendations and National Immunisation Program funding depend on age and other eligibility criteria. It can be useful whether you are ready to try now or are thinking about pregnancy in the coming months. What Is It? Preconception care may include reviewing medicines, vaccination status, chronic conditions, family history, lifestyle and any previous pregnancy complications. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural-tube defects; iodine advice depends on circumstances including thyroid health. Regular medicine review before pregnancy Past pregnancy complications Questions about supplements and screening Should I Be Concerned? Arrange an appointment if you take regular medicines, have diabetes, high blood pressure, epilepsy or a mental health condition, have difficulty conceiving, or have a history of miscarriage. Planning scans and screening Questions about medicines or vaccination Bleeding, severe symptoms or changes in pregnancy wellbeing Should I Be Concerned? text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Weight & Healthy Lifestyle Healthy Weight Management Weight and health are connected, but a number on the scale does not describe the whole person. A helpful plan focuses on wellbeing, sustainable habits and any medical issues affecting weight. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Weight and health are connected, but a number on the scale does not describe the whole person. A helpful plan focuses on wellbeing, sustainable habits and any medical issues affecting weight. What Is It? Body weight can be influenced by genetics, medicines, sleep, hormones, living circumstances, activity and food access. Evidence-based care avoids blame and extreme dieting, and considers blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol, mobility and quality of life. Weight affecting blood pressure or diabetes Unexplained weight change Questions about evidence-based support Should I Be Concerned? Book a conversation if weight changes unexpectedly, affects health or movement, or if repeated attempts to change weight have been distressing. Rapid unintentional weight loss, persistent fatigue or other symptoms deserve medical review rather than a diet plan alone. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Sudden weight changes with severe illness, confusion, dehydration or other emergency symptoms require urgent assessment. Weight management appointments are not a substitute for treatment of acute illness or disordered eating symptoms that threaten safety. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess relevant health risks and possible medical contributors, review medicines and work with you on realistic goals. Options may include dietitian or exercise-physiology support, sleep assessment or medicines when clinically indicated. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is there one best diet for everyone? No. A sustainable approach that meets nutritional needs and fits a person’s circumstances is preferable to rigid fad diets. Will my GP prescribe weight-loss medicines? Medicines may be considered for some patients after assessment of indications, benefits, risks and alternatives; they are not suitable for everyone. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Weight & Healthy Lifestyle When Should I Speak To A GP About Weight? You can raise weight concerns with a GP without waiting for a crisis or a particular body-mass-index result. The conversation should be respectful and related to your own health goals. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction You can raise weight concerns with a GP without waiting for a crisis or a particular body-mass-index result. The conversation should be respectful and related to your own health goals. What Is It? Changes in weight may reflect food and activity patterns, medicines, sleep, stress or health conditions. A useful appointment considers not only weight but your medical history, metabolism, mood and whether eating behaviours are becoming distressing. Unexpected weight changes Concern about restrictive diets Weight affecting mobility or long-term health Should I Be Concerned? Arrange a visit for unplanned gain or loss, weight-related joint pain or breathlessness, diabetes risk, or concerns about restrictive eating. Tell your GP if you would prefer not to have your weight announced during the consultation. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe dehydration, fainting, chest pain or acute illness require urgent care. If food restriction, purging or an eating disorder is affecting physical safety, seek prompt medical assessment rather than following generic weight advice. How Can a GP Help? A GP can ask permission before discussing weight, arrange targeted tests if needed and offer a health-focused plan. Referrals may include a dietitian, psychologist or other professional depending on the circumstances. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Will every consultation involve a weigh-in? Not necessarily. Explain your preferences and ask how a measurement would affect clinical decisions. Can medicines affect weight? Yes. Several medicines and medical conditions can influence weight. A GP can review possible contributors without stopping treatment abruptly. The most useful changes are specific, achievable and revisited over time. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Health advice can feel overwhelming when it is presented as a long list of rules. The most useful changes are specific, achievable and revisited over time. What Is It? Healthy lifestyle habits include food variety, movement, sleep, stress management, avoiding tobacco and moderating alcohol. Their benefits extend beyond weight to cardiovascular health, mental wellbeing, mobility and diabetes prevention. Starting movement after inactivity Questions about healthy eating patterns Managing sleep and stress alongside health goals Should I Be Concerned? Talk to a GP if health advice conflicts with a medical condition, medicines or physical limits, or if you are unsure where to begin. Breathlessness, persistent fatigue, pain or mood changes may need assessment before a new exercise plan. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Chest pain, fainting during exertion or severe breathlessness requires urgent assessment; call 000 for life-threatening symptoms. A new activity routine should not be used to push through significant warning signs. How Can a GP Help? A GP can prioritise one or two changes that matter for your health, check risk factors and refer for tailored support. Setting a realistic follow-up date is often more valuable than making a dramatic change that cannot be sustained. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I have to change everything at once? No. Gradual and consistent changes are often easier to maintain, especially when supported by realistic goals. Is exercise safe with a chronic condition? Often yes, but the type and intensity should be tailored to your condition, medicines and current fitness. title: Menopause Symptoms Explained
description: Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Menopause & Midlife Health Menopause Symptoms Explained Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing. People experience different combinations of symptoms and not everyone needs treatment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing. People experience different combinations of symptoms and not everyone needs treatment. What Is It? Menopause is defined retrospectively after twelve months without a menstrual period in a person not using hormonal treatment that changes bleeding. Perimenopause is the transition leading up to that point. Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, vaginal dryness, mood changes and irregular cycles can occur. Hot flushes and night sweats Irregular bleeding or vaginal symptoms Sleep and mood changes around midlife Should I Be Concerned? Arrange a GP appointment if symptoms affect quality of life, if bleeding is heavy or unusual, or if periods stop unusually early. New bleeding after menopause needs assessment rather than being assumed to be a normal hormonal change. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe bleeding with fainting or collapse requires urgent assessment. Chest pain, stroke-like symptoms or severe breathlessness are emergencies: call 000. Do not explain every new symptom as menopause without considering other causes. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review the symptom pattern and health history, discuss non-hormonal strategies and menopausal hormone therapy where appropriate, and assess other health considerations such as bone and heart health. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I always need a hormone blood test? Not always. For many people over 45, the symptom and menstrual history is more useful than a single hormone result. Can symptoms start before periods stop? Yes. Perimenopause can involve symptoms and irregular bleeding before the final menstrual period. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Menopause & Midlife Health HRT Discussions With Your GP Menopausal hormone therapy, sometimes called HRT, may help with troublesome menopausal symptoms. Deciding whether it is suitable should be a shared discussion rather than a standard prescription for everyone. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Menopausal hormone therapy, sometimes called HRT, may help with troublesome menopausal symptoms. Deciding whether it is suitable should be a shared discussion rather than a standard prescription for everyone. What Is It? Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) can relieve hot flushes, night sweats and some vaginal symptoms. Options include patches, gels, tablets and local vaginal treatments. People with a uterus who use systemic oestrogen usually need endometrial protection with a progestogen. Persistent hot flushes or night sweats Questions about patches or vaginal treatment Reviewing hormone therapy risks and side effects Should I Be Concerned? Speak with a GP if symptoms significantly affect sleep or daily activities, you are considering MHT or you have questions about alternatives. Personal factors such as clotting history, unexplained bleeding, cardiovascular disease and certain cancers influence suitability. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Unexpected heavy bleeding, severe chest pain, stroke symptoms or sudden breathlessness require urgent care. If you develop symptoms suggesting a blood clot while using hormone therapy, seek immediate medical assessment. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review benefits, risks, preparation type and dose, as well as alternatives and follow-up. Regular reassessment considers symptom benefit, side effects, medical history and changing preferences; MHT is not prescribed solely to prevent chronic disease. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is HRT suitable for everyone? No. Benefits and risks depend on age, medical history, type of hormone treatment and personal circumstances. Are patches and tablets identical? No. Routes of administration have different considerations, including clotting risk, which your GP can explain. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Menopause & Midlife Health Mental Health & Menopause Mood changes during midlife can be confusing, particularly when they happen alongside disrupted sleep and physical menopausal symptoms. The connection deserves assessment without assuming hormones explain everything. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Mood changes during midlife can be confusing, particularly when they happen alongside disrupted sleep and physical menopausal symptoms. The connection deserves assessment without assuming hormones explain everything. What Is It? Hormonal changes during perimenopause may coincide with anxiety, irritability, low mood, reduced concentration or sleep problems. Work, caregiving, previous mental health conditions and other medical factors can also influence how a person feels. Mood changes with hot flushes Difficulty sleeping and concentrating Persistent anxiety, irritability or low mood Should I Be Concerned? Book an appointment if mood or anxiety symptoms persist, interfere with relationships or work, or affect your ability to cope. Share sleep changes, menstrual history, medicines and whether symptoms occur alongside hot flushes or night sweats. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? If you are at immediate risk of harming yourself or another person, call 000 or attend an emergency department. New severe confusion, chest pain or major physical symptoms must not be attributed to menopause alone. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review mental and physical health together, discuss talking therapies, sleep support, non-hormonal treatment and whether MHT may help menopausal symptoms. Follow-up is important to assess what is improving and what still needs care. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can menopause cause anxiety? Hormonal changes and sleep disruption may contribute, but anxiety can have other causes that also deserve assessment. Can I discuss mental health and menopause in one GP appointment? Yes. Ask reception whether a longer appointment would allow enough time for a fuller discussion.
